title: The Chapel Door
story:
The morning sun rose warm over the tile roofs of Aldea San Gabriel. Yesterday's freshly sanded cedar stool sat securely on the dry dirt floor of his shed, its three short legs steady and even. James tested it with a gentle press of his palm, admiring the golden sheen of the wood under the morning light. Satisfied, he stepped out into the open workshop, where Don Tadeo was already busy dry-fitting a heavy cedar door frame destined for the village chapel down the lane.

James had learned the quiet sound of cedar being planed. James had learned the rough scratch of coarse sand-cloth on unrefined grain. James had learned the rich, resinous scent that filled the air whenever the old carpenter worked. Without needing to be asked, James reached for a small wooden mallet and tapped a wooden dowel snugly into place along the lower joint, earning a approving nod from the old man. Together, they lifted the heavy frame and carried it down the narrow cobblestone lane.

As they walked through the heart of the village, neighbors called out greetings from their doorways. An elderly woman washing corn at a stone basin waved a damp hand; a young boy trailing a wooden hoop called out softly. James walked beside Don Tadeo, balancing a small box of wooden pegs against his chest, feeling less like a visitor passing through and more like a familiar shadow along the worn adobe walls. When they arrived at the chapel lane, Don Tadeo showed James how to align the door frame plumb against the old wall, using a simple lead plumb-bob on a string.

By late afternoon, the old door frame was firmly set in place, sealed tight against the mountain winds. Sitting on the low stone steps of the chapel, James watched the golden light stretch across the valley floor below. He pulled out his green sea-glass and looked through it, watching the sunlit dust motes float lazily through the chapel doorway. Day sixty-seven had arrived gently in this quiet corner of the world, and for the first time since leaving the canopy, the horizon did not feel like something he had to run toward, but something he was living inside.
